# Abstract

Colonial Paraguay encompassed 415.304 km² of subtropical riverine forest, savanna woodland and arid thorny scrub in the heart of South America, structured by the navigable courses of the Paraguay and Paraná rivers. Between the founding of the Spanish fort of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción in 1537AD and the declaration of provincial independence in May 1811AD, the region underwent an intricate demographic evolution characterized by profound ethnic reconstitution, frontier violence, institutionalized communal servitude and extraordinary monastic urbanization. Initial Spanish settlement was founded not on mineral extraction but on polygynous kinship alliances with the Cario-Guaraní peasantry, producing a rapid transition from autonomous horticultural lineages to a dense, bilingual mestizo population alongside institutionalized encomienda labour.

Across the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, the demographic geography of the province fractured into four distinct zones: the agricultural Asunción core; the embattled eastern frontier of Guairá, subjected to devastating slave raids by São Paulo bandeirantes and repeatedly relocated westward; the semi-autonomous commonwealth of thirty Jesuit Guaraní reducciones straddling the Paraná and Uruguay river basins; and the sovereign indigenous domain of equestrian and hunter-gatherer nations across the Gran Chaco Boreal. Supported by an unusually rich primary census record, including early encomienda inspections, the exhaustive annual mission registers (anuas), and the late colonial headcounts of Juan Francisco de Aguirre (1782AD) and Félix de Azara (1799AD), this study reconstructs provincial numbers across nine canonical benchmarks.

Aggregate regional population fell from an estimated 257.000 in 1537AD (comprising 85.000 in the Asunción core, 68.000 in Guairá, 62.000 in the southern Paraná missions and 42.000 in the Chaco) to a contact nadir of 155.000 by 1680AD. Subsequent expansion was driven by the demographic consolidation of the Jesuit missions, which reached a historic peak of 72.000 within the modern Paraguayan sector in 1732AD (and over 141.000 across all thirty missions), lifting provincial numbers to 177.000 before catastrophic epidemic mortality between 1732AD and 1739AD erased nearly one-third of the mission populace. The royal expulsion of the Society of Jesus in 1767AD unleashed secular mismanagement and widespread Guaraní dispersion, yet robust eighteenth-century mestizo natural increase and agrarian settlement in the central valleys restored total provincial population to 162.000 in 1782AD, 174.000 in 1799AD and 193.000 by 1811AD.

# Historical Demography of the Paraguayan Province

The historical demography of colonial Paraguay occupies an anomalous position in the Spanish American empire. Lacking silver, mercury or gold, the province of Paraguay, initially designated the Gobernación del Río de la Plata y del Paraguay, was transformed into an isolated inland enclave following the reorientation of imperial logistics towards Potosí and the Pacific coast [@garavaglia1983mercado; @moramerida1973historia]. The territorial framework established between 1537AD and 1811AD comprised 415.304 km² organized along two grand riverine arteries: the southward-flowing Río Paraguay, dividing the eastern subtropical forests from the arid scrub of the Gran Chaco Boreal, and the upper Río Paraná, flowing south and west across basalt cataracts before joining the Paraguay at Paso de Patria.

Colonial population dynamics unfolded within four structural divisions: the central core around Asunción, Cordillera and Paraguarí (19.779 km²); the eastern and northern march of Villarrica, Guairá, San Pedro and Concepción (98.670 km²); the Jesuit mission territory along the Paraná, Tebicuary and Uruguay basins (48.127 km²); and the sovereign Chaco frontier (248.728 km²). Table \ref{tab:benchmarks} presents the regional trajectory reconstructed across nine benchmark years.

The underlying spatial modelling for this study operates on a 5-arcminute raster grid comprising 5.280 active terrestrial cells within the provincial boundary. Demographic densities are estimated through non-stationary Matérn kriging, interpolating localized historical census returns against fluvial proximity, soil fertility and known settlement coordinates. The regional gazetteer compiles 220 validated historical settlements, encompassing colonial towns, Franciscan pueblos de indios, Jesuit reducciones, river ports and frontier garrisons.

By integrating quantitative returns from parish registers, episcopal visitations and colonial censuses, the reconstruction illuminates the contrasting demographic regimes of the province: the high-fertility peasant reproduction of the central valleys, the severe mortality crises of the Jesuit mission towns, and the low-density stability of the unconquered Chaco nations.

## Ecological Zones and Settlement Geography

The physical geography of Paraguay conditioned both pre-contact indigenous settlement patterns and the spatial trajectory of Spanish colonization [@kleinpenning2003paraguay; @mendes2024guaranis]. The province straddled four distinct ecological zones:

- The Atlantic humid forest (*Selva Paranaense*) extended across eastern Guairá, Caaguazú and Alto Paraná, dominated by massive canopies of lapacho (*Handroanthus*), cedro (*Cedrela fissilis*) and yerba mate (*Ilex paraguariensis*). This biome received 1.600 to 2.000 mm of annual rainfall, supporting rich volcanic and basalt soils favourable for intensive horticultural clearings.
- The central parkland and savanna (*Sabana con Palmares*) occupied the depression between the Cordillera de los Altos and the Río Tebicuary, characterized by karanday palms (*Copernicia alba*), gallery forests and fertile crystalline soils that formed the primary agrarian heartland of Asunción.
- The southern wetland complex (*Esteros de Ñeembucú*) encompassed the low-lying lacustrine plains formed by the confluence of the Paraguay, Tebicuary and Paraná rivers, offering natural pasturage for Jesuit and secular cattle ranching alongside seasonal flooding hazards.
- The semi-arid thorn forest (*Chaco Xerofítico*) west of the Río Paraguay spanned 248.728 km² of alluvial clays and calcic soils, dominated by quebracho colorado (*Schinopsis*), palo santo (*Bulnesia sarmientoi*) and algarrobo (*Prosopis*), characterized by prolonged droughts, high evapotranspiration and scarce potable groundwater.

These environmental parameters dictated the spatial clustering of the 220 catalogued settlements, confining over ninety percent of the colonial population to the well-watered eastern biomes within fifty kilometres of navigable rivers.

The pedology of eastern Paraguay was dominated by deep, red ferralsols and nitisols developed over Mesozoic basalt formations of the Paraná basin [@pastore2025considerat]. These terra roxa soils possessed high natural fertility and moisture retention, supporting continuous maize, manioc and tobacco cultivation without fallowing when enriched by alluvial silt deposits. Conversely, the hydromorphic gleysols of the Ñeembucú lowlands impeded deep rooting, restricting agricultural clearings to elevated islands (*islas de monte*) surrounded by seasonal wetlands.

## Methodological Reconstruction and Data Sources

The longitudinal demographic series constructed for Colonial Paraguay bridges three distinct institutional and archival recording traditions across three centuries:

First, early sixteenth-century conquistador chronicles, muster rolls and encomienda repartimientos document the initial contact and transition to servitude. Domingo Martínez de Irala conducted the first formal division of encomiendas in 1556AD, partitioning approximately 20.000 Cario tributaries among 320 conquistadors in Asunción [@moramerida1973historia]. This record was expanded by royal cosmographer Juan López de Velasco in 1574AD and codified by the extensive judicial inspection of Visitor Francisco de Alfaro between 1609AD and 1611AD, whose reports detailed the demographic decay of encomienda villages under personal service [@necker1979indiens; @telesca2009arcilla].

Second, the Society of Jesus established an annual census apparatus without equal in the early modern colonial world. Beginning in 1610AD and continuing uninterrupted until 1767AD, each mission superior compiled an annual status report (*carta anua*) and nominal census (*padrón de almas*), enumerating every resident by household, age category (*párvulos* under age nine, *doctrina* children aged ten to fourteen, and adults), civil status, and baptismal, matrimonial and mortuary tallies [@maeder1980evolucion; @jackson2008demographic]. These registers, preserved in the Archivo General de la Nación in Buenos Aires and the Archivum Romanum Societatis Iesu in Rome, provide precise annual population series for the eight Paraguayan reducciones.

Third, late Bourbon administration generated province-wide nominal and statistical headcounts. Bishop Manuel Antonio de la Torre conducted an exhaustive diocesan visitation between 1758AD and 1761AD, followed in 1782AD by the general census commanded by Viceroy Juan José de Vértiz and transcribed by boundary commissioner Juan Francisco de Aguirre [@aguirre1949diario; @maeder1992misiones]. The colonial sequence culminated in the 1799AD census and demographic geography of Don Félix de Azara, whose thorough parish-by-parish registers record the agrarian distribution, ethnic proportions and family sizes of the late colonial population on the eve of independence [@azara1847descripcion; @azara1904geografia].

## Fluvial Geography and Pre-Contact Guaraní Substratum

Prior to the arrival of European expeditions, eastern Paraguay was settled by horticultural Guaraní lineages grouped into territorial clusters known as *guaras* [@susnik1965indio; @telesca2009arcilla]. These populations inhabited longhouses (*malocas*) housing extended patrilineages of fifty to one hundred individuals, encircled by palisades and manioc, maize and sweet potato swiddens cleared from the subtropical Atlantic and gallery forests. Settlement density was highest along the Paraguay River bluffs and the fertile crystalline soils of the central depression running from Asunción southeast towards the Tebicuary River.

The pre-contact Guaraní population in the territory defined by the colonial provincial mask is estimated at approximately 215.000 sedentary cultivators, supplemented by 42.000 nomadic and semi-sedentary foragers in the Gran Chaco Boreal, yielding an aggregate baseline of 257.000 persons in 1537AD [@susnik1965indio; @candela2026resistenci]. Guaraní agrarian practice was adapted to cyclical relocation, as tropical soils depleted after two to three harvests, necessitating systematic clearing of new plots.

This residential mobility, coupled with institutionalized kinship mechanisms based on reciprocal gift exchange and marriage alliances (*tovajá* or brother-in-law relationship), directly shaped the initial European encounter [@potthast2020mestizaje]. Guaraní horticulturalists cultivated bitter and sweet manioc (*mandi'o*), maize (*avati*), beans (*kumanda*), pumpkins (*andai*) and sweet potatoes (*jety*), supplementing agriculture with riverine fishing and forest hunting. The environmental productivity of the riverine bluffs permitted localized population densities exceeding 4 persons per km² along the Paraguay and Tebicuary rivers, while the interior serranías supported lower densities around 1 to 1,5 persons per km².

The hydrological regime of the Río Paraguay imposed clear limits on permanent human occupancy. Annual floodwaters (*crecientes*), cresting between April and July, inundated vast alluvial flats up to thirty kilometres from the primary channel, forcing both pre-contact lineages and Spanish colonial founders to build exclusively atop elevated sandstone terraces (*albardones*) and volcanic bluffs. This topography determined the selection of Asunción's red cliffs, as well as the high terrace locations of Altos, Areguá, Ypané and Encarnación.

## Spanish Conquest, Asunción and Kinship Alliances (1537AD to 1580AD)

The permanent European colonization of the Río de la Plata basin began in August 1537AD, when Juan de Salazar y Espinosa founded the wooden palisade of Nuestra Señora de la Asunción on a red bluffs overlooking a natural bay of the Río Paraguay. Unlike the violent subjugation of the Inca and Aztec states, the early settlement of Asunción was established through an alliance between Spanish conquistadors and the local Cario-Guaraní leaders, who sought military allies equipped with iron weapons against their traditional enemies, the Guaycuruan raiders of the Chaco [@candela2026resistenci; @ganson2003guarani].

The Guaraní provided the Spaniards with food supplies and women in accordance with *cuñadazgo*, the traditional indigenous custom whereby the exchange of women established obligations of reciprocal military and labour assistance [@potthast1996indias; @potthast2020mestizaje]. Because Spanish female immigration to Paraguay was virtually non-existent, conquistadors established extensive polygynous households, prompting contemporary ecclesiastical chroniclers to characterize early Asunción as the "Paradise of Mahomet" (*Paraíso de Mahoma*).

This sexual and social union produced a biological and cultural transformation: within a generation, the indigenous elite of Asunción was superseded by a mestizo cohort known as *mancebos de la tierra*, who were raised by Guaraní-speaking mothers while inheriting Spanish patriarchal legal status [@potthast2020mestizaje; @ito2012with]. These bilingual mestizos formed the demographic foundation of subsequent provincial expansion, serving as the founders and settlers of secondary colonial towns across the Río de la Plata basin, including Santa Cruz de la Sierra (1561AD), Santa Fe (1573AD), Corrientes (1588AD) and the refoundation of Buenos Aires in 1580AD.

Concurrently, European epidemic introductions began to erode indigenous numbers. Outbreaks of smallpox, measles and respiratory ailments swept through the central valleys in 1558AD, 1560AD and 1572AD. By 1580AD, the population of the central Asunción district had contracted from 85.000 to 54.000, while Guairá fell from 68.000 to 46.000, pulling provincial numbers down to 187.000.

## Encomienda, Pueblos de Indios and Colonial Restructuring (1580AD to 1630AD)

As the initial reciprocity of *cuñadazgo* dissolved under growing Spanish demands for continuous agrarian and extractive labour, the colonial administration codified compulsory indigenous servitude through the encomienda [@necker1979indiens; @telesca2009arcilla]. Unlike the tribute encomienda prevalent in the Andes and New Spain, the Paraguayan encomienda was characterized by compulsory personal service (*servicio personal*). It was divided into two distinct legal and socio-spatial categories:

1. *Originarios*: Indigenous individuals and nuclear families bound permanently to the rural estates (*chácaras* and *estancias*) of Spanish encomenderos. They performed agricultural labour, cattle herding and domestic service without cash wages, losing direct ties to autonomous communal villages [@susnik1965indio; @ioris2024indigeneit].
2. *Mitayos*: Male tributaries aged eighteen to fifty belonging to designated indigenous communal villages (*pueblos de indios*). They were compelled to perform rotational unpaid labour for their encomendero for two months annually, primarily in the harvesting and transport of yerba mate from remote forests [@garavaglia1983mercado; @moramerida1973historia].

To organize and control the dispersed indigenous population, Franciscan friars, led by Fray Luis de Bolaños, established the first *pueblos de indios* across the central valley between 1580AD and 1600AD [@necker1979indiens; @telesca2009arcilla]. Settlements such as Altos (1580AD), Ypané (1580AD), Guarambaré (1580AD), Tobatí (1580AD), Itá (1585AD) and Yaguarón (1587AD) concentrated thousands of Guaraní into grid-plan villages centered on a plaza, church and communal municipal council (*cabildo indígena*). These towns preserved communal land tenure while functioning as reservoirs of rotational *mitayo* labour for the Asunción oligarchy.

The spatial segregation imposed by the pueblos de indios was intended by the Franciscan friars to insulate the indigenous populace from the moral and physical exploitation of Spanish secular society [@necker1979indiens]. Within each pueblo, municipal government was exercised by an indigenous *corregidor* and *alcaldes*, overseen by a resident Spanish *administrador* or parish priest. This dual administration fostered the preservation of indigenous craft traditions while channelling communal surplus directly into colonial trade networks.

The brutality of yerba mate gathering (*beneficio de la yerba*) in the pestilential forests of the northern and eastern frontiers imposed severe demographic penalties. Tributaries suffered from exhaustion, malnutrition, snakebites and tropical fevers, depressing indigenous fertility and accelerating the decline of communal villages [@garavaglia1983mercado]. When Visitor Francisco de Alfaro promulgated his famous ordinances in 1611AD (*Ordenanzas de Alfaro*), which formally abolished personal service and mandated money wages, the Paraguayan settlers vigorously resisted, ensuring that personal service persisted in practice throughout the colonial period [@necker1979indiens; @acemoglu2001colonial].

# The Jesuit Guaraní Reducciones (1609AD to 1767AD)

The demographic development of colonial Paraguay was fundamentally altered by the arrival of the Society of Jesus. In 1604AD, the Jesuit Province of Paraguay was established, encompassing a vast territorial jurisdiction that extended from Buenos Aires to Santa Cruz de la Sierra [@jackson2008demographic; @sarreal2014guarani]. Seeking to convert the indigenous population beyond the reach of the encomienda, Fathers Lorenzana and San Martín founded San Ignacio Guazú in 1609AD, the mother mission of the famous thirty Jesuit Guaraní reducciones.

## Foundation, Bandeirante Raids and Southern Guaraní Relocation

The early Jesuit missions were distributed across three geographic sectors: Guairá, located east of the Paraná River in modern Paraná state, Brazil; the Itatín region in modern Mato Grosso do Sul; and the Tapé and Paraná-Uruguay river basins [@maeder1980evolucion; @ganson2003guarani]. In Guairá, Jesuit fathers established thirteen thriving missions between 1610AD and 1628AD, congregating over 100.000 Guaraní souls [@maeder1980evolucion; @kuhne2025churches].

This monastic demographic concentration attracted the predations of slave-hunting expeditions from São Paulo, known as *bandeiras*. Led by figures such as Manuel Preto and Antonio Raposo Tavares, heavily armed *bandeirantes* attacked the unprotected reducciones between 1628AD and 1632AD, capturing tens of thousands of Christian Guaraní for sale to coastal sugar plantations in Rio de Janeiro and Bahia [@ganson2003guarani; @sarreal2014guarani].

In response, Father Antonio Ruiz de Montoya organized an epic mass migration in 1631AD: over 12.000 Guaraní fled south down the Paraná River in hundreds of wooden canoes, abandoning thirteen towns. Surviving disease, hunger and cataracts at the Guaíra Falls, the refugees resettled along the Tebicuary, Paraná and Uruguay rivers [@maeder1980evolucion; @jackson2015demographic].

Securing royal permission from Philip IV in 1639AD to arm the mission Guaraní with firearms, the Jesuits organized an indigenous army. At the historic Battle of Mbororé in March 1641AD, the Guaraní militia decisively defeated a major *bandeira* on the Uruguay River, halting Paulist territorial expansion and permanently establishing the fortified frontier of the thirty missions [@ganson2003guarani; @wucherer2019from].

## Demographic Zenith, Sanitary Regimes and the Anuas Records (1680AD to 1732AD)

Following the stabilization of the southern frontier, the thirty reducciones underwent sustained demographic expansion. The mission territory constituted a distinct institutional commonwealth: the crown granted the Jesuits exemption from encomienda obligations in exchange for an annual head tax paid directly to the royal treasury [@sarreal2014guarani; @jackson2008demographic]. The missions were organized as communal agrarian municipalities: land was partitioned into *tupambaé* (God's property, farmed collectively for communal storage, social welfare, widows and church maintenance) and *abambaé* (individual family plots) [@sarreal2014guarani; @ganson2023gender].

The Jesuits maintained administrative registers (*anuas*, *padrones* and baptismal, marriage and death rolls), creating a continuous longitudinal demographic record of exceptional detail in colonial Latin America [@maeder1984poblacion; @jackson2008demographic]. Every resident was registered by lineage (*cacicazgo*), household and age group. Medical regimes included communal quarantine infirmaries (*enfermerías*), clean water provision, systematic vaccination using early variolation techniques by the late eighteenth century, and generous distribution of beef from enormous communal cattle herds (*estancias*), ensuring caloric and protein intakes well above contemporary European rural averages [@sarreal2014guarani; @jackson2015demographic].

Within the eight missions situated in the modern territory of Paraguay (San Ignacio Guazú, Santa María de Fe, Santa Rosa de Lima, Santiago, San Cosme y Damián, Itapúa [Encarnación], Santísima Trinidad del Paraná, and Jesús de Tavarangüé), population rose from 46.000 in 1620AD to 58.000 in 1680AD and attained a peak of 72.000 in 1732AD [@maeder1984poblacion]. Across the entire thirty-mission commonwealth, total population reached 141.182 souls in 1732AD, representing the densest concentration of indigenous population south of the Tropic of Capricorn.

## Age Structure, Fertility Regimes and Morbidity in the Reducciones

Demographic analysis of the Jesuit mission registers reveals a distinctive vital regime characterized by high natural fertility offset by extreme epidemic mortality spikes [@jackson2008demographic; @sarreal2014guarani]. The missionaries actively promoted early and universal marriage to align with Christian moral strictures and to maximize population numbers: young women typically married between the ages of fourteen and sixteen, and young men between sixteen and eighteen.

As a consequence of early nuptiality and abundant dietary protein provided by communal cattle distributions, crude birth rates in the missions routinely ranged between 48 and 62 per 1.000 inhabitants during inter-epidemic periods [@maeder1984poblacion; @jackson2015demographic]. Completed family size averaged between six and eight live births per mother. However, infant and child mortality was exceptionally severe: deaths of *párvulos* (children under age ten) accounted for 52 to 64 percent of all burials recorded in normal years, reflecting the endemic prevalence of gastrointestinal infections, parasitic disorders and neonatal tetanus.

Parish baptismal rolls (*libros de bautismos*) document pronounced seasonal rhythms in conceptions. Conception tallies peaked systematically between April and June, immediately following the completion of the collective maize and yerba mate harvests, and dipped during the hottest summer months of January and February [@maeder1984poblacion].

This demographic regime produced an expansive, bottom-heavy age pyramid, with children under age fifteen comprising 42 to 48 percent of the total mission populace. In the absence of epidemic disease, the reducciones expanded at natural growth rates of 2,2 to 3,4 percent per annum, explaining the rapid recovery observed between 1680AD and 1732AD. Yet this dense, immunologically naïve population living in compact urban blocks was acutely vulnerable to crowd infections, ensuring that periodic epidemic incursions transformed steady natural increase into sudden demographic collapse.

## Epidemic Mortality and Comunero Disruptions (1732AD to 1739AD)

Prior to the devastating crisis of the 1730s, the mission communities had already suffered substantial losses during the 1718-1719AD smallpox epidemic, which carried away over 15.000 Guaraní across the thirty towns [@maeder1984poblacion]. Rapid natural reproduction restored numbers over the subsequent decade, carrying the population to its historic peak of 141.182 in 1732AD.

This demographic peak was abruptly terminated by an overlapping series of exogenous epidemiological shocks and political crises. In 1732AD, a severe smallpox pandemic penetrated the missions from Buenos Aires, followed in 1735AD and 1736AD by typhus and measles [@jackson2008demographic; @maeder1984poblacion]. Between 1732AD and 1739AD, over 40.000 Guaraní died across the thirty missions. In the Paraguayan sector, population collapsed from 72.000 to approximately 48.000, representing a net loss of one-third of the community.

Compounding this epidemiological devastation was the political turbulence of the Comunero Revolts (*Revolución Comunera*, 1721-1735AD) [@whigham1991politics; @potthast2020mestizaje]. The Asunción agrarian elite and town council (*cabildo*), envious of the vast landholdings, duty-free yerba mate exports and autonomous military force of the Jesuits, rose in armed rebellion against royal authority under leaders José de Antequera y Castro and Fernando Mompox.

The rebels invaded the mission frontier, confiscating cattle and sacking border settlements. Crown forces, supported by thousands of Guaraní mission infantry, ultimately crushed the rebellion at the Battle of Tavapy in 1735AD, but the logistical strain, field mortality and agricultural neglect exacerbated the epidemic death toll [@sarreal2014guarani].

Following the restoration of order, the missions experienced demographic recovery, regaining a population of 56.000 in the Paraguayan sector by 1767AD (and 105.000 across all thirty towns), though they never re-attained their 1732AD demographic zenith [@maeder1984poblacion; @sarreal2014guarani].

## The 1767AD Expulsion and Guaraní Demographic Dispersion

In February 1767AD, King Charles III issued the Pragmatic Sanction expelling the Society of Jesus from all Spanish realms. In Paraguay, the decree was executed in 1768AD by Governor Bucareli. While Franciscan, Dominican and Mercedarian friars assumed spiritual administration of the reducciones, temporal governance and economic administration were transferred to royal civil administrators (*administradores temporales*) [@sarreal2013disorder; @maeder1992misiones].

The results were catastrophic. Unscrupulous administrators dismantled the communal livestock reserves, mismanaged trade accounts, and subjected the Guaraní to abusive commercial contracts [@sarreal2013disorder; @susnik1979indio2]. Deprived of the paternalistic security and communal cohesion of the Jesuit regime, thousands of mission Indians abandoned the towns. This movement did not represent physical extinction, but rather an accelerated demographic dispersion:

- Guaraní families migrated northward into the central Asunción depression and Cordillera, assimilating into the expanding mestizo peasantry as free wage labourers, tenant farmers (*agregados*) or rural craftsmen [@susnik1979indio2; @telesca2009arcilla].
- Skilled artisans, carpenters and boatbuilders migrated downriver to Corrientes, Santa Fe, Entre Ríos and Buenos Aires, providing vital labour for the booming port economy of the newly established Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata (1776AD) [@whigham1991politics; @sarreal2013disorder].
- Others took refuge across the eastern forest frontiers or were incorporated into the growing private cattle estates (*estancias*) of the southern plains [@ioris2024indigeneit].

By 1782AD, the population residing within the eight Paraguayan missions had plummeted to 34.000; by 1799AD it stood at 31.000, and by 1811AD at 32.000, less than half of its mid-eighteenth-century level [@maeder1992misiones; @azara1904geografia].

Contemporary petitions by Guaraní cabildos sent to Buenos Aires documented the systemic breakdown of the mission economy, with caciques lamenting the loss of community cotton stocks, musical instruments and sacred vessels under corrupt temporal administrators [@sarreal2013disorder; @ganson2003guarani]. This administrative collapse transformed formerly cohesive monastic towns into depopulated settlements surrounded by overgrown orchards.

# Sub-Regional Demographic Dynamics

The trajectory of colonial Paraguay was shaped by pronounced geographical divergence across its four principal sub-regions. Figure \ref{fig:hero-spatial} illustrates their spatial extents and settlement distributions.

## Central Core: Asunción, Central and Paraguarí

The central sub-region (19.779 km²) comprised the historical heartland of Spanish settlement, encompassing Asunción, the fertile agrarian valleys of the Cordillera, Lake Ypacaraí, and the cattle plains of Paraguarí. After contracting from 85.000 in 1537AD to an all-time nadir of 38.000 in 1680AD under the combined impact of virgin-soil epidemics and intense encomienda labour extraction, this core zone initiated a powerful demographic recovery [@potthast2020mestizaje; @velazquez1965paraguay].

Unlike the mission district, where demographic expansion was halted after 1767AD, the central core experienced sustained natural increase throughout the eighteenth century, expanding to 46.000 in 1732AD, 54.000 in 1767AD, 64.000 in 1782AD, 74.000 in 1799AD and 86.000 by 1811AD. Growth was fueled by high marital fertility among the mestizo rural population, declining epidemic mortality outside the crowded missions, and the absorption of dispersed Guaraní migrants from the decaying reducciones [@susnik1990vision; @telesca2009arcilla].

Asunción grew into a bustling commercial and administrative river port of 13.800 inhabitants by 1811AD, while surrounding satellite towns such as San Lorenzo (3.599), Luque (3.260), Capiatá, Itauguá and Pirayú expanded into flourishing agricultural market centers [@cardozo2019downtown; @anon2019asuncion]. These agricultural communities produced manioc, maize, sugarcane, tobacco and fruits, feeding the urban markets and supplying trade flotillas descending the river system.

The Franciscan pueblos de indios within this central zone (Altos, Itá, Yaguarón, Tobatí, Atyrá, Guarambaré and Ypané) maintained distinct communal identities throughout the eighteenth century [@telesca2009arcilla]. While their legal status under the encomienda bound their adult males to rotational mitayo labour, the preservation of communal lands (*tierras comunales*) allowed these towns to maintain stable populations ranging from 1.200 to 2.800 inhabitants each. These communities served as repositories of indigenous crafts, including pottery in Itá, woodcarving in Yaguarón, and cotton and bromelia (*karaguata*) textile weaving in Altos.

## The Eastern and Northern March: Guairá, Villarrica and Concepción

The northeastern zone (98.670 km²) formed a contested borderland between the Spanish empire and Portuguese Brazil. Originally centered east of the Paraná River around Ciudad Real del Guairá (founded 1556AD) and Villa Rica del Espíritu Santo (founded 1570AD), this region contained an estimated 68.000 inhabitants in 1537AD. Following the devastating bandeirante raids of 1628-1632AD, the Spanish town of Villarrica was forced to relocate repeatedly westward, moving seven times across five decades before finally taking root at its modern location in 1682AD [@kleinpenning2003paraguay; @mendes2024guaranis].

Population in this zone touched a low of 26.000 in 1680AD. During the eighteenth century, recovery was fostered by two institutional developments. In the south, Villarrica consolidated into a premier agricultural and yerba mate commercial center, reaching 6.200 inhabitants by 1811AD.

In the north, royal governors initiated a policy of defensive military recolonization to counter the raids of equestrian Mbaya-Guaicurú bands and Portuguese territorial incursions from Mato Grosso [@kleinpenning2003paraguay; @wucherer2019from]. Governor Agustín Fernando de Pinedo founded Villa Real de la Concepción on the upper Paraguay River in 1773AD, anchoring northern agrarian settlements that grew to 3.945 residents by 1811AD, alongside newly established parishes at San Pedro de Ycuamandiyú (1786AD) and Rosario (1787AD). Regional population expanded steadily to 32.000 in 1767AD, 36.000 in 1782AD, 42.000 in 1799AD and 48.000 on the eve of independence.

Further east along the cordilleras of Mbaracayú and Amambay, Spanish authorities established fortified yerba mate collecting centers, notably Villa de San Isidro Labrador de Curuguaty in 1716AD [@garavaglia1983mercado]. Curuguaty served as the primary processing and packaging depot for the lucrative yerba trade, gathering thousands of seasonal labourers and mestizo frontiersmen who harvested wild yerba trees in the dense subtropical selva before transporting the bales by mule train to the river port of Asunción.

## The Missions District: Paraná and Uruguay Basins

The mission sub-region (48.127 km²) encompassed the southern rolling grasslands and wetlands of Misiones, Itapúa, Ñeembucú and the Alto Paraná river bluffs. Reconstructed population rose from 62.000 in 1537AD to 72.000 in 1732AD, supported by the monumental urbanism, planned sanitation and disciplined cattle-ranching of the Jesuit reductions. Following the epidemic disasters of the 1730s and the 1767AD expulsion, the demographic trajectory inverted: the population declined to 56.000 in 1767AD, 34.000 in 1782AD, and stabilized at 31.000 to 32.000 between 1799AD and 1811AD [@maeder1992misiones; @sarreal2014guarani].

Despite the flight of indigenous families, the urban footprint established by the Jesuits persisted. San Ignacio Guazú remained the leading settlement with a peak census of 6.774, followed by the riverine port of Pilar (6.414), Encarnación (4.652), Santa Rosa de Lima (4.380) and Santiago (4.170).

The strategic fortress-port of Pilar de Ñeembucú, founded in 1779AD by Governor Pedro Melo de Portugal at the confluence of the Paraguay and Bermejo rivers, became the primary customs station controlling fluvial commerce entering and exiting the province [@whigham1991politics; @kleinpenning2003paraguay]. Pilar gathered Spanish and mestizo merchants, boatbuilders and military garrisons, growing rapidly from a frontier fort into a major urban center that challenged the commercial dominance of Asunción in the southern trade network.

## The Gran Chaco Boreal Frontier

West of the Paraguay River extended the vast, semi-arid expanse of the Gran Chaco Boreal (248.728 km²), comprising nearly sixty percent of the provincial territory. Throughout the colonial period, the Chaco remained an unconquered indigenous territory dominated by non-sedentary nations belonging to the Guaycuruan, Mataco-Guaicurú and Enlhet-Enxet linguistic families [@susnik1965indio; @wucherer2019from].

The equestrian Mbaya-Caduveo and Abipón, possessing herds of feral horses adopted from Spanish coastal strays in the late sixteenth century, established military hegemony over the plains, conducting swift amphibious and cavalry raids against Spanish estates east of the river [@candela2026resistenci]. Riverine Payaguá bands utilized fleets of dug-out war canoes to dominate the channel of the Río Paraguay, ambushing Spanish merchant flotillas sailing between Asunción and Corrientes until decisively pacified in the late eighteenth century.

Spanish presence in the Chaco was restricted to isolated defensive garrisons and ephemeral mission outposts. In 1792AD, Governor Joaquín Alós y Bru founded Fuerte Borbón (later renamed Fuerte Olimpo) in the far northern Chaco to block Portuguese naval patrols descending the Río Paraguay from Cuiabá. Overall Chaco population contracted gradually from approximately 42.000 in 1537AD to 33.000 in 1680AD and stabilized at 27.000 between 1799AD and 1811AD, maintaining a low demographic density of 0,11 persons per km² [@susnik1990vision; @azara1847descripcion].

## The Presidio Network and Riverine Defences

To safeguard the riverine transport route connecting Asunción with the Río de la Plata estuary and to check Portuguese incursions from the Upper Paraguay, the late Bourbon governors constructed an integrated line of coastal forts and presidios [@kleinpenning2003paraguay; @wucherer2019from]. These military foundations directly shaped demographic settlement along the western river boundary:

- Fuerte Borbón, established in 1792AD on the right bank of the Upper Paraguay, garrisoned forty infantrymen and artillery pieces on a rocky promontory, observing Portuguese naval movements from the neighbouring Brazilian fortress of Forte Novo de Coimbra (founded 1775AD). Borbón established sovereign Spanish possession over the northern Chaco, housing soldiers, gunsmiths and indigenous auxiliaries.
- Remanso del Castillo, positioned south of Asunción, guarded the western river crossing against equestrian Guaycuru incursions, providing a fortified redoubt where crossing cattle herds and trade carretas gathered under escort.
- San Carlos del Apa, founded in 1794AD along the Río Apa frontier, anchored a line of cavalry outposts that shielded northern estancias in Concepción from both Mbaya raiders and Portuguese bandeirante cattle rustlers.

These garrisons operated in coordination with local urban militias composed of armed mestizo chacreros. By securing river channels against aquatic Payaguá raiders, the presidio network enabled merchant smacks (*chalanas*) and timber rafts to navigate between Asunción and the southern ports with negligible armed escort after 1780AD.

The fluvial naval patrol (*flotilla de resguardo*) deployed armed piraguas and gun launches from the Asunción naval yard (*arsenal*). These vessels conducted regular reconnaissance along the Manduvirá and Tebicuary rivers, deterring hostile crossings and escorting commercial balsas laden with yerba mate and timber to the deep-water anchorages of Pilar and Corrientes [@whigham1991politics].

# Eighteenth-Century Recovery and Late Colonial Censuses

During the final decades of the eighteenth century, the demographic recording of Paraguay achieved unprecedented empirical rigor through two comprehensive censuses commissioned by the Bourbon administration.

## The Aguirre (1782AD) and Azara (1799AD) Censuses

Following the creation of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata in 1776AD and the implementation of the Intendancy system in 1782AD, Viceroy Juan José de Vértiz ordered a general census of the newly designated Intendancy of Paraguay (*Intendencia del Paraguay*). The returns were analysed and transcribed by naval commissioner Juan Francisco de Aguirre, who served in Asunción between 1784AD and 1796AD as part of the Spanish-Portuguese boundary demarcation commission [@aguirre1949diario; @maeder1992misiones]. Aguirre documented a total provincial population of 162.000 souls in 1782AD, recording detailed breakdowns by civil status, ethnicity (*españoles*, *indios*, *mestizos*, *pardos* and *negros*) and parish jurisdictions.

Seventeen years later, Don Félix de Azara, an accomplished naturalist, geographer and boundary commissioner who resided in Paraguay for over a decade, synthesised civil and ecclesiastical padrones to produce the landmark 1799AD provincial census [@azara1847descripcion; @azara1904geografia]. Azara counted 174.000 inhabitants within provincial borders, observing the rapid expansion of the free mestizo population and noting that Guaraní remained the universal spoken language across all social classes, in sharp contrast to other Spanish American administrative capitals [@ito2012with; @potthast2020mestizaje]. Table \ref{tab:late-censuses} compares sub-regional populations, densities and ethno-social profiles recorded by these primary registers.

The census of 1799AD revealed that seventy-nine percent of the provincial population east of the Paraguay River resided in agricultural smallholdings and rural parishes rather than formal towns. Family units averaged 5,8 persons, reflecting high marital fertility and low infant mortality compared to urban centers in the viceroyalty. The indigenous population recorded in the former Jesuit reducciones and Franciscan pueblos de indios constituted twenty-six percent of the provincial total, while free mestizos and criollos comprised sixty-two percent, and enslaved or free afro-descendants (*pardos* and *negros*) made up the remaining twelve percent [@aguirre1949diario; @candela2026resistenci].

## Ethno-Demographic Stratification on the Eve of Independence

The ethno-demographic composition recorded on the eve of independence exhibited singular features within the Spanish colonial empire [@potthast2020mestizaje; @telesca2009arcilla]. Unlike the rigid racial caste hierarchies (*sistema de castas*) enforced in viceregal Lima or Mexico City, social differentiation in Paraguay was moderated by the pervasive use of the Guaraní language across all socio-economic strata. While Spanish served as the language of royal decrees, legal petitions and ecclesiastical correspondence, Guaraní was the universal domestic tongue of Spanish governors, Franciscan missionaries, mestizo estancieros, afro-descendant militiamen and communal tributaries alike [@ito2012with].

Afro-descendant populations occupied an integral position in late colonial society [@candela2026resistenci; @telesca2009arcilla]. While black slaves were imported through Buenos Aires to work as domestic servants in Asunción and agricultural hands on Jesuit and private estancias, the crown established autonomous free black communities along the frontier. Most prominent was San Agustín de la Emboscada, founded in 1740AD northeast of Asunción. Emboscada was settled by runaway slaves (*cimarrones*) from Portuguese Brazil who were granted royal manumission in exchange for hereditary military service in defending the Cordillera frontier against Mbaya cavalry raids [@candela2026resistenci]. By 1799AD, Emboscada had grown into a thriving agricultural and garrison town of over 1.800 free afro-descendant inhabitants.

The free mestizo and criollo peasantry (*chacreros*) formed the demographically expanding core of the late colonial province. Possessing small family holdings (*piquetes*) carved from municipal common lands, these families practiced diversified polyculture centered on manioc, maize, tobacco and citrus orchards. This agrarian structure, characterized by the relative absence of massive latifundia and the widespread availability of fertile subsistence land, provided the economic basis for robust demographic resilience and sustained natural increase throughout the late eighteenth century [@velazquez1965paraguay; @pastore2025considerat].

## Agrarian Expansion, Yerba Mate and Independence Eve (1811AD)

The final decades of colonial rule witnessed an economic reorientation driven by free trade reforms (*Comercio Libre*, 1778AD) and the opening of the Buenos Aires port to global commerce [@garavaglia1983mercado; @whigham1991politics]. Paraguay expanded its exports of processed yerba mate, cured leaf tobacco and river timber down the Paraguay-Paraná river system, generating substantial trade surpluses and stimulating domestic agriculture.

Rural families established smallholder farmsteads throughout the central valleys, cultivating manioc, maize, sugarcane and citrus. By 1811AD, total provincial population reached 193.000 inhabitants, reflecting sustained natural increase that had completely overcome the contact demographic decline [@velazquez1965paraguay; @whigham1999rosetta]. When Governor Bernardo de Velasco capitulated to the patriotic revolution in Asunción on 14-15 May 1811AD, establishing independent Paraguay under a republican junta, the new nation possessed an unusually homogeneous social fabric: a cohesive, bilingual Guaraní-Spanish mestizo population rooted in family agriculture and fortified by three centuries of frontier resilience [@potthast2020mestizaje; @pastore2025considerat].

The spatial equilibrium established in 1811AD concentrated nearly forty-five percent of the provincial population within the compact central core of Asunción, Central and Paraguarí (86.000 inhabitants), producing an average density of 4,35 persons per km². The northern and eastern frontier supported 48.000 persons (0,49 persons per km²), anchored by Villarrica and Concepción. The former mission district held 32.000 persons (0,66 persons per km²), while the sovereign Chaco remained at 27.000 persons (0,11 persons per km²). This demographic baseline provided the human foundations for the autonomous, state-directed development that characterized early nineteenth-century independent Paraguay.

In subsequent decades, this demographic stability underpinned the consolidation of the republican regime under Dr. José Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia (1814-1840AD) [@middleton2021britain; @whigham1991politics]. By sealing provincial borders against regional civil wars and establishing state ranches (*Estancias de la Patria*), independent Paraguay relied directly on its colonial demographic inheritance: a self-sufficient peasantry rooted in communal and family land tenure, capable of sustaining national sovereignty in complete geographical isolation.
